name: Owa
confidence_why: Known only second-hand, as quoted in another work.
catalog_citation: Mellow, Greg. 2014. A Dictionary of Owa: A Language of the Solomon Islands. Pacific Linguistics 639. Berlin/Boston: De Gruyter Mouton. Grammar sketch, ch. 1 'Phonology', sec. 1.3 'Stress and Intonation', p. 5 (chapter DOI 10.1515/9781614513612.2); read first-hand from the Google Books publisher-preview p. 5.
catalog_quote: Stress is indicated in this section by an apostrophe before the stressed syllable. Stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable of the word stem, for example, au.’ra.gi ‘married’, and ka.’ri.nga ‘fungus’. Rarely, the stress in a three syllable stem will fall on the antepenultimate syllable, for example, ‘fe.fe.ne ‘female’, and ‘ma.re.fa ‘no’. Where a small word such as a demonstrative follows a longer word, the stress may migrate, as if the two words were one phonetic word. It is difficult to properly describe where stress will fall in a word since stress in a word can depend on its position in a phrase.

new_statements.quote: Usually, the second-to-last syllable is stressed in the Owa language, e.g., auragi /ɐʊ.ˈɾɐ.gɪ/ 'married'. But occasionally the antepenultimate (third-to-last) syllable is stressed, as in fefene /ˈfɛ.fɛ.nɛ/ 'female'. However, stress placement depends on the context, specifically where it is located in the sentence; therefore, it is difficult to predict stress patterns in Owa.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: line 107 '=== Stress ===', line 109 carries the three quoted sentences verbatim once wiki templates ({{lang}}, {{IPA}}, {{gloss}}, {{sfn}}) are stripped: 'Usually, the second-to-last syllable is stressed.. auragi /ɐʊ.ˈɾɐ.gɪ/ married.. occasionally the antepenultimate.. fefene /ˈfɛ.fɛ.nɛ/ female.. stress placement depends on the context.. difficult to predict stress patterns in Owa.' Minor locator nit: only the first two sentences carry {{sfn|Mellow|2013|p=5}}; the third (context/unpredictability) sentence is unfootnoted, so that caveat is the Wikipedia editor's wording with no page cite. Identity: the article's infobox has iso3=stn, glotto=owaa1237, dialects Tawarafa/Owa Raha/O…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Default word stress on the penultimate syllable; some words carry antepenultimate stress instead (e.g. fefene 'female'); realised stress also shifts with position in the sentence, so the author (as summarised) treats it as not fully predictable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing reported in the accessible (second-hand) text.
new_statements.exceptions: Antepenultimate stress in some words (fefene /ˈfɛ.fɛ.nɛ/ 'female'); sentence-position effects on stress placement.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement with an explicit caveat that placement varies with sentence context (phrase-level interaction); examples are citation forms. Second-hand summary only — Mellow's own wording on p. 5 not seen (note: 'penultimate' does not occur in Mellow's text per Google Books index, so his phrasing differs).
new_statements.identity_note: All statements concern Owa [stn] = Glottolog owaa1237 as described by Mellow (dialects Tawarafa, Owa Raha, Owa Riki per Wikipedia summarising Mellow). Owa forms a dialect chain with Kahua [agw] (kahu1239); Mellow's data are from Santa Ana (Owa Raha) / Star Harbour area. No dialect-specific stress differences reported in what was accessible.
